title: The lifeguard, swimming pool & supervision
description: Prevent incidents, understand your pool and keep every part of your zone under observation.

lessons.title: Your role as a lifeguard
lessons.summary: Prevention comes first. Be ready to intervene, rescue and give first aid.

blocks.heading: The job in one sentence
blocks.body: Keep people safe through continuous observation, clear communication and early action. Rescue is essential, but noticing a problem before it becomes an emergency is just as important.
bullets: Observe the whole assigned area, including the pool bottom, surface and surrounding activity.
Educate swimmers and enforce rules consistently.
Respond immediately to a person in difficulty and summon the team.
Provide care within your training, then report and record accurately.

blocks.heading: Professional standards
blocks.body: Arrive fit, prepared and ready to work. Wear the designated uniform and carry the equipment your site requires, such as a whistle and communication device. Keep personal phones and unrelated conversations away from supervision. Tell your supervisor if illness, medication, fatigue or another issue could affect safe work.

blocks.heading: Interview practice
blocks.body: Describe a time you noticed a risk early. Explain what you saw, the calm action you took and how you checked that everyone remained safe. Good answers show observation, teamwork and accountability, rather than claiming you can manage every situation alone.

lessons.title: Clear communication & difficult conversations
lessons.summary: Use a calm explanation, a clear instruction and a check that the swimmer understands.

blocks.heading: A useful sequence
blocks.body: Get attention, give the instruction, explain the safety reason and check the response. A whistle attracts attention; it does not tell a swimmer what to do next. Use plain language, suitable gestures and the agreed site signals.

blocks.heading: Keep supervision effective
blocks.body: Make conversations brief while on duty. Pass on urgent information, but maintain observation. If a complaint needs sustained attention, request a colleague or supervisor to deal with it without creating a gap in cover.
bullets: Listen without interrupting or becoming defensive.
Remain respectful, even when a customer is frustrated.
Offer a safe alternative when possible.
Escalate threats, repeated refusal or unresolved complaints through the site procedure.

blocks.heading: Try saying it
blocks.body: “Please walk on poolside. The wet surface can be slippery.” This gives a specific action and a reason. Avoid vague instructions, sarcasm or arguing across the pool.

blocks.heading: Whistle signals in the supplied course
blocks.body: The slides recommend one short blast for a pool user’s attention, two short blasts for another lifeguard’s attention, three short blasts for emergency action and one long blast when clearing the pool. Confirm the signals in your own NOP and follow a signal with the necessary instruction. Hand signals, radios and alarms also need site-specific training.

lessons.title: Induction, competence & training records
lessons.summary: Your certificate is the starting point; safe work also needs site knowledge and regular practice.

blocks.heading: Know your workplace
blocks.body: Induction should introduce the building, pool depths and features, rescue equipment, alarms, operating procedures and your role in an emergency. Do not assume a new pool works like the pool where you trained.

blocks.heading: Maintain competence
blocks.body: Attend ongoing training and competency checks. Practise realistic incidents with the team so that responsibilities, communication and equipment use are familiar under pressure. Keep your own record of the date, venue, duration, trainer, subjects and outcomes.

blocks.heading: Before an interview or practical check
blocks.body: Bring your qualification evidence and training record. Be ready to explain how you would learn a new site, report a concern and maintain your skills. For renewal requirements, check the current RLSS qualification information and your certificate dates.

lessons.title: Responsibilities, guidance & safe systems
lessons.summary: Understand what you must do personally and what the pool operator must organise.

blocks.heading: Shared responsibility
blocks.body: The operator must assess risks, organise safe working arrangements and provide suitable information, instruction, training and supervision. Lifeguards must take reasonable care, cooperate with safety arrangements and report hazards. Follow the procedures you have been trained to use.

blocks.heading: Law and guidance
blocks.body: HSE pool guidance helps operators meet their duties; it is not itself a separate swimming-pool law. Staffing and controls depend on the actual pool and activities. Learn the purpose of relevant arrangements, including hazardous-substance control, safe manual handling, first-aid provision and protective equipment.

blocks.heading: When something is unsafe
blocks.body: Act within your role to prevent harm, notify the supervisor and record the concern through the agreed process. Never continue with an unfamiliar task or faulty equipment simply because you feel pressure to keep the session running.

lessons.title: PSOP, NOP & EAP
lessons.summary: Separate everyday operating instructions from the plan for an emergency.

blocks.heading: The two parts
blocks.body: The Pool Safety Operating Procedures (PSOP) bring together the Normal Operating Plan/Procedures (NOP) and the Emergency Action Plan (EAP). The NOP explains safe routine operation. The EAP sets out the response when normal safe operation is disrupted.

blocks.heading: Find it in the NOP
blocks.body: Use the NOP for pool layout and depths, staffing, zones, rotations, admission rules, maximum occupancy, equipment checks, communication and safe working instructions.

blocks.heading: Find it in the EAP
blocks.body: Use the EAP for incidents such as a casualty in the water, serious injury, fire, chemical release, loss of water clarity, overcrowding and evacuation. Know who raises the alarm, calls emergency services, brings equipment, clears the area and meets responders.

blocks.heading: Check your understanding
blocks.body: You need the depth at a particular feature: look in the NOP. The water becomes too cloudy for effective observation: act under the EAP and alert the supervisor. Do not invent a universal signal or evacuation route; learn your site’s arrangements.

lessons.title: Hazards, risk & dynamic assessment
lessons.summary: Spot what can cause harm, assess who is exposed and choose a practical control.

blocks.heading: Three different ideas
blocks.body: A hazard has the potential to cause harm. Risk considers how likely that harm is and how serious it could be. A control reduces the risk. For example, a slippery walkway is a hazard; separating users from the area while it is cleaned is a control.

blocks.heading: Look at the whole environment
blocks.body: Think about premises and utilities, tasks and activities, and people. Pool depth, drains and lighting interact with cleaning, inflatables, crowding, swimming ability and behaviour.

blocks.heading: Dynamic assessment
blocks.body: Conditions change during a shift. Notice the change, reassess its effect, take the action your role allows and tell the supervisor. A written assessment is useful only when staff also respond to what is happening now.
bullets: Has glare hidden part of the bottom?
Has an activity changed the way swimmers move through the zone?
Is a swimmer tiring or relying on the wall to stay afloat?
Is the agreed cover still enough for the conditions?

lessons.title: Safeguarding, inclusion & admission rules
lessons.summary: Respect different needs while applying the same commitment to safety.

blocks.heading: Safeguarding concerns
blocks.body: Follow your site’s safeguarding policy. Listen calmly, take concerns seriously and report promptly to the designated person. Record facts and the person’s own words where relevant. Do not promise secrecy, investigate the allegation yourself or share details with people who do not need them.

blocks.heading: Inclusive practice
blocks.body: Ask how you can help instead of making assumptions about disability, language, age or background. Explain rules clearly and use the available support. Learn how hoists and accessible routes operate before assisting someone.

blocks.heading: Admission and supervision
blocks.body: Apply the operator’s child-admission policy, including the required adult supervision and any activity restrictions. There is no single ratio to invent for every pool. A parent’s presence does not remove your duty to supervise your zone.

blocks.heading: After a difficult incident
blocks.body: Use the debrief and support offered by the operator. Distress can affect rescuers and witnesses. Seek professional support if symptoms persist or affect daily life; asking for help is compatible with being a competent lifeguard.

lessons.title: Pool types, depths & features
lessons.summary: Translate the pool’s design into the risks you need to watch.

blocks.heading: Know the layout
blocks.body: Learn the dimensions, gradients, depth changes, entrances, exits and blind spots. Competition pools, diving pools, leisure pools and outdoor pools create different supervision problems. Do not infer depth from the shape or colour of the pool.

blocks.heading: Equipment changes the risk
blocks.body: Starting blocks, lane ropes and backstroke flags can be misused. Steps and handrails must remain accessible. Hoists require trained operation and checks. Moveable floors and booms require their own safe system, restricted controls and correct depth signage.

blocks.heading: Leisure features
blocks.body: Waves and moving water can tire a swimmer or move them out of their depth. Slides require spacing, permitted riding positions and a clear landing area. Diving boards need controlled access and a clear water area. Follow manufacturer and site rules; switch off or stop a feature through the EAP when necessary.

blocks.heading: Outdoor considerations
blocks.body: Watch for weather, cold, glare and changing visibility. Know the site plan for lightning or deteriorating conditions. Never substitute a general internet rule for the operator’s assessed procedure.

lessons.title: Visibility, drains & entrapment
lessons.summary: Effective observation means seeing beneath the surface as well as above it.

blocks.heading: Visibility is a safety condition
blocks.body: Glare, reflections, turbulence, steam, crowding and poor water clarity can hide a person. Assess the whole zone, including the floor. Report and act immediately if the assigned position no longer gives effective observation; use the site’s approved response.

blocks.heading: Entrapment hazards
blocks.body: Damaged or missing drain covers and suction outlets can trap hair, clothing or body parts. Keep users away, notify the supervisor and follow the emergency isolation procedure if a person is trapped. Do not enter hazardous plant areas or operate unfamiliar controls.

blocks.heading: Walls and guttering
blocks.body: A weak swimmer pulling along the gutter can unknowingly move into deep water. Intervene early and guide them to a suitable area. Prevent tampering with covers, outlets, ropes and features.

lessons.title: Activities, inflatables & safe set-up
lessons.summary: Every change of activity needs appropriate equipment, supervision and access rules.

blocks.heading: Before a session
blocks.body: Check the activity risk assessment and operating instructions. Confirm trained staffing, lifeguard positions, user ability restrictions, bather numbers, entry and exit points and emergency access.

blocks.heading: Inflatables
blocks.body: Design and positioning can obscure swimmers and create fall, collision or entrapment risks. Use the required anchoring, clearances, inspections and emergency arrangements. Set-up and removal need trained staff, enough assistance and safe lifting methods.

blocks.heading: Galas, parties and lessons
blocks.body: Noise can mask communication; ropes and equipment change movement routes; excited groups can ignore hazards. Maintain admission rules and clear responsibilities between lifeguards, teachers, coaches and organisers. An instructor is not automatically a substitute for lifeguard cover.

lessons.title: Opening checks, cleaning & chemicals
lessons.summary: Keep routine work safe without taking attention away from supervision.

blocks.heading: Before opening
blocks.body: Follow the checklist for the pool and its surroundings, rescue aids, alarms, first-aid equipment, AED readiness, signs and access routes. Record defects and report them. Equipment that is present but unusable does not provide effective protection.

blocks.heading: Cleaning and handling
blocks.body: Use the trained method, suitable protective equipment and barriers or warning signs. Organise cleaning so that supervision remains effective. Assess the load and route, use handling aids and get enough help for heavy equipment.

blocks.heading: Chemical safety
blocks.body: Use only substances and equipment you are authorised and trained to handle. Follow the product information and local COSHH assessment. Never mix chemicals or improvise a spill clean-up. Isolate the area and raise the alarm under the EAP if there is a release or exposure.

blocks.heading: Closing checks
blocks.body: Check that customers have left and complete the site’s equipment, access and security checks. Only sign a check that you have actually performed. If a safety-critical check cannot be completed or fails, report it and follow the escalation procedure.

lessons.title: Swimmer ability, behaviour & early intervention
lessons.summary: Notice small changes before they become a rescue.

blocks.heading: Watch ability and behaviour together
blocks.body: A person may be confident but unable to cope with depth, waves or tiredness. Pay attention to weak swimmers, young children, unfamiliar users and anyone showing signs of distress. Avoid assumptions based on appearance or swimming aids.

blocks.heading: Intervene early
blocks.body: Stop pushing, ducking, fighting, unsafe diving and dangerous informal teaching. Discourage prolonged underwater distance swimming and breath-holding contests. Explain a safe alternative and escalate persistent unsafe behaviour.

blocks.heading: Illness or intoxication
blocks.body: Unsteady movement or unusual behaviour may reflect a medical problem as well as alcohol or drugs. Keep the person safe, summon assistance and assess the situation within your training. Do not let a potentially unsafe swimmer enter the pool while the concern is unresolved.

lessons.title: Zones, scanning & vigilance
lessons.summary: Use a deliberate observation pattern and keep the whole zone in view.

blocks.heading: Know your responsibility
blocks.body: Learn the zone boundaries and the coverage arrangements in the NOP. Observe the surface, the water below it, the bottom and the relevant poolside area. Know how your view overlaps with colleagues and where obstructions can develop.

blocks.heading: Natural Scan:20
blocks.body: The supplied course slides describe continuous scanning and require the operator to ensure a lifeguard can reach any point in their zone within 20 seconds. This is not permission to leave gaps between scans. The zone must be designed, staffed and tested so that observation and response are realistic.

blocks.heading: Active observation
blocks.body: Scan systematically and interpret what you see. Change your focus between individuals and the whole area. Look for a swimmer making little progress, a low head position, unusual stillness or submersion. Do not wait for shouting or waving; distress may be quiet.

blocks.heading: Control distractions
blocks.body: Do not allow conversation, phones, secondary duties or watching a single activity to take over your attention. Use agreed rotation and breaks to support concentration. Report fatigue and changes in visibility.

blocks.heading: Technology supports you
blocks.body: Detection and surveillance systems can help the team, but they need trained use and an understood response. Do not assume a device will notice a casualty for you or replace required direct supervision.

lessons.title: Rotation, handover & team readiness
lessons.summary: A handover is complete only when the next lifeguard has taken responsibility.

blocks.heading: Maintain continuous cover
blocks.body: Follow the rotation route and timings in the NOP. The incoming lifeguard should establish an effective view and acknowledge responsibility before the outgoing lifeguard leaves. Keep the exchange short and focused.

blocks.heading: Timing in the supplied slides
blocks.body: The course recommends changing positions every 15, 20 or 30 minutes, with no more than 30 minutes at one static position. It recommends no longer than 60 minutes poolside, or 90 minutes in exceptional circumstances in the pool hall. Learn the actual rota and limits in your NOP; report if cover or breaks are not working.

blocks.heading: Pass on what matters
blocks.body: Highlight a swimmer needing extra observation, an equipment fault, an altered activity, changes in numbers or visibility, and any instructions from the supervisor. Avoid casual conversation while either lifeguard is responsible for the zone.

blocks.heading: Emergency teamwork
blocks.body: Practise specific roles: rescuer, pool cover, alarm and emergency call, equipment retrieval, crowd control and ambulance access. A clear instruction to a named person is easier to act on than a general shout for help.

title: Intervention, rescue & emergency action
description: Recognise difficulty early, choose a safe rescue and work effectively with your team.

lessons.title: Recognise a casualty & act early
lessons.summary: A person in trouble may be quiet, still or making movements that look almost normal.

blocks.heading: Recognise a change
blocks.body: Look for loss of progress, an unusually vertical position, repeated submersion, a pained expression or someone floating without a clear purpose. A concerned bystander can be the first indication. Investigate immediately if you are unsure.

blocks.heading: Different presentations
blocks.body: A tired swimmer may respond to instructions and reach an aid. A non-swimmer may be unable to call out. An injured or medically unwell swimmer can deteriorate rapidly. An unresponsive casualty may be at the surface, under the water or on the bottom.

blocks.heading: Match action to urgency
blocks.body: A non-critical intervention prevents an accident: give a clear instruction and monitor compliance. A critical intervention responds to immediate danger to life: activate the EAP and carry out a rescue without delay. Never wait for the casualty to match a textbook picture.

lessons.title: Choose a safe rescue & summon help
lessons.summary: Use the safest effective method and make the team aware of the emergency.

blocks.heading: Before contact
blocks.body: Assess danger, casualty condition, distance, depth, available equipment and help. Raise the alarm using your site’s signal. Delegate the emergency call and equipment retrieval where colleagues are present.

blocks.heading: Rescue options
blocks.body: Where effective, give instructions and offer a reaching or throwing aid from a secure position. Enter the water when required by the situation and your training. Take the appropriate rescue aid and keep the casualty in view.

blocks.heading: Stay within trained skills
blocks.body: Close contact with a panicking swimmer can endanger the rescuer. Use the approach, distancing and defensive actions practised with your trainer. A written guide cannot check your grip, buoy placement or swimming technique; rehearse these in supervised practical training.

lessons.title: Water entry, approach & rescue aids
lessons.summary: Choose the entry for the depth, conditions and casualty.

blocks.heading: Select the entry
blocks.body: The taught entries include slide-in, step/walk-in, straddle and shallow dive. Suitability depends on known depth, obstacles, space, the equipment you carry and whether a spinal injury is suspected. Never dive into unknown or unsuitable depth.

blocks.heading: Approach with control
blocks.body: Keep the casualty in sight and communicate if they can respond. Use a stroke that allows observation and effective progress. Manage straps and lines so that they do not become an entanglement hazard.

blocks.heading: Use aids as trained
blocks.body: Reaching poles and torpedo buoys help bridge distance and support a casualty. Check them before use, understand their limits and practise placing and securing them. Do not rely on an improvised technique learned only from reading.

lessons.title: Towing, assistance & getting out
lessons.summary: Protect the airway, communicate and use enough trained help.

blocks.heading: During the tow
blocks.body: Use the trained tow appropriate to the casualty and rescue aid. Keep their mouth and nose clear, monitor their response and maintain control. Reassure a responsive casualty and get support at the exit point.

blocks.heading: Select an exit
blocks.body: A responsive casualty may be able to use steps or an assisted walk-out. A casualty unable to help may need an assisted lift or other taught extraction. The pool design, injuries, body size and available staff affect the choice.

blocks.heading: Team handling
blocks.body: One person should coordinate the lift with clear commands. Prepare the route and landing area. Use the site’s handling technique and equipment; do not strain to complete a lift alone when help is required. Once out, assess immediately and start appropriate care.

lessons.title: Suspected spinal injury in the water
lessons.summary: Save life first, then minimise movement and prevent further injury.

blocks.heading: When to suspect it
blocks.body: A dive, collision, fall or impact to the head or neck can injure the spine. Look for pain, altered sensation, weakness, unusual posture, confusion or an unresponsive casualty after an impact. Absence of obvious pain does not rule out injury.

blocks.heading: Airway takes priority
blocks.body: Keep the face clear of the water. If the casualty is unresponsive, the supplied course material prioritises immediate removal and assessment on poolside. Spinal restriction must not delay treatment when resuscitation is required.

blocks.heading: Conscious casualty
blocks.body: Reassure them, discourage unnecessary movement and summon trained assistance. Use the spinal support and extraction method you have been taught, such as the practised head-splint/vice-grip and board procedures where appropriate. Do not force alignment or attempt unfamiliar manoeuvres.

blocks.heading: Practical rehearsal
blocks.body: Practise face-down recognition, the turn, team communication, support and extraction with your instructor. These are physical skills assessed through performance; reading and a quiz cannot certify competence.

lessons.title: Drowning & immediate resuscitation
lessons.summary: Get the casualty out safely and restore breathing without delay.

blocks.heading: Priorities after removal
blocks.body: Check responsiveness, call 999/112 immediately or delegate the call, open the airway and assess breathing. If unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing after drowning, give five initial rescue breaths, then continue the appropriate CPR sequence.

blocks.heading: Breaths matter
blocks.body: Drowning deprives the body of oxygen. Trained rescuers should provide ventilations as well as compressions. Do not delay CPR trying to drain water from the lungs. If fluid or vomit obstructs ventilation, clear the airway using your trained method and resume promptly.

blocks.heading: AED and follow-up
blocks.body: Bring an AED as soon as possible, dry the chest quickly and follow its instructions. Continue care and monitoring even if the casualty improves. Report the circumstances, estimated submersion information if known, symptoms and treatment to ambulance staff.

lessons.title: Major emergencies & evacuation
lessons.summary: Know your role before an alarm sounds.

blocks.heading: The EAP is specific to the site
blocks.body: Know the alarm, communication chain, who takes control and who calls emergency services. Follow the plan for overcrowding, poor clarity, disorderly behaviour, fire, chemical release, lighting failure, structural damage and severe weather.

blocks.heading: Evacuation
blocks.body: Use a safe route and assembly point. Consider wet, cold swimmers, children in lessons and people who need assistance. Do not direct people past a chemical release or other danger. Maintain communication and account for people according to the procedure.

blocks.heading: Contamination and missing children
blocks.body: Report bodily-fluid or faecal contamination and follow closure instructions; cleaning and reopening decisions belong to trained responsible staff. Treat a missing-child report urgently: activate the search procedure, including immediate attention to the water, without abandoning required pool cover.

blocks.heading: Make an effective emergency call
blocks.body: Give the exact location and access route, what happened, number of casualties, responsiveness and breathing, current hazards and treatment underway. Follow the call handler’s instructions and arrange for someone to meet responders.

lessons.title: Prepare for your practical check & interview
lessons.summary: Rehearse safe decisions and honest examples, then check the employer’s format.

blocks.heading: Two-day refresher plan
blocks.body: Day one: revise supervision and emergency procedures, practise a safety paper, then review every explanation. Day two: revise CPR and first aid, practise the second paper and rehearse interview answers. Arrange supervised practical practice if available; do not attempt rescue drills alone.

blocks.heading: Expect local variation
blocks.body: An employer may assess swimming, rescues, CPR, first aid, customer communication and knowledge of site procedures. Ask the recruiter for the format and what to bring. The supplied sample is a qualification theory paper, so it cannot guarantee the questions in a recruitment test.

blocks.heading: Prepare three examples
blocks.body: Use Situation, Task, Action and Result to explain teamwork, a difficult conversation and spotting a safety risk. If you lack work experience, use a genuine example from training, study or volunteering. Explain when you would escalate rather than bluffing.

blocks.heading: Before you attend
blocks.body: Check your certificate, identification, arrival time, swim kit and any requested records. Sleep, eat and hydrate. Tell the assessor if something affects your ability to complete an exercise safely.

title: CPR, AED & first aid
description: Recognise life-threatening conditions and revise the actions that protect life.

lessons.title: First-aid priorities, consent & hygiene
lessons.summary: Preserve life, prevent deterioration and work within your training.

blocks.heading: Start safely
blocks.body: Check danger to yourself, the casualty and bystanders. Request help and the appropriate equipment. The team must arrange continuing pool supervision while care is given. Use gloves and other suitable protection without delaying urgent life-saving action.

blocks.heading: Consent and dignity
blocks.body: Explain what you intend to do and ask permission when the casualty can respond. If they cannot consent, provide necessary emergency care in their best interests. Respect privacy and share relevant information with those providing care.

blocks.heading: Prevent infection
blocks.body: Use appropriate barriers, wash hands and dispose of contaminated items safely. Sharps belong in an approved sharps container; do not pick them up with bare hands or recap needles. Follow the exposure procedure if you are injured or contaminated.

blocks.heading: After treatment
blocks.body: Replace used supplies, record the incident accurately and ensure appropriate onward care. Do not diagnose beyond your competence or give medication outside your training and site arrangements.

lessons.title: Primary survey & recognising cardiac arrest
lessons.summary: Unresponsive means call for help immediately. Gasping is not normal breathing.

blocks.heading: Assess in a clear order
blocks.body: Check safety and responsiveness. If unresponsive, call 999/112 immediately, preferably with another team member or a speakerphone. Request the AED. Open the airway and assess breathing for no more than ten seconds while the call connects.

blocks.heading: Recognise abnormal breathing
blocks.body: Occasional gasps, snoring-like noises, slow laboured breaths or panting in an unresponsive person are not reassurance. If breathing is absent or abnormal, assume cardiac arrest and start CPR. A brief seizure can occur at the start of an arrest; reassess breathing after it stops.

blocks.heading: Structured assessment
blocks.body: For an ill or injured casualty, identify and treat immediate threats, including catastrophic bleeding. Use Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure to structure ongoing assessment. Do not let a detailed history or head-to-toe examination delay urgent care.

blocks.heading: Current guidance
blocks.body: The 2025 RCUK sequence calls emergency services as soon as unresponsiveness is identified. The supplied May 2026 adult flowchart follows this sequence. Confirm the latest practical sequence with your trainer.

blocks.heading: The chain of survival
blocks.body: Recognise the emergency and call early, start effective CPR, use an AED promptly and hand over for professional treatment and recovery care. Each action supports the next; do not delay one while waiting for the others.

lessons.title: Adult CPR: quality matters
lessons.summary: Use effective compressions, appropriate breaths and minimal interruption.

blocks.heading: Compressions
blocks.body: Kneel beside the chest on a firm surface. Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone with the other hand on top. Keep arms straight, compress 5–6 cm at 100–120 per minute and let the chest fully recoil.

blocks.heading: Breaths and rhythm
blocks.body: If trained to ventilate, give 30 compressions followed by two breaths. Each breath should take about one second and make the chest begin to rise. Keep interruptions short. If unable to give breaths, continue compressions and follow the call handler.

blocks.heading: Keep going
blocks.body: Follow AED prompts. Continue until the casualty shows clear signs of life and normal breathing, emergency professionals take over or direct you to stop, you cannot continue, or the scene becomes unsafe. Change compressors with minimal interruption when help is available.

blocks.heading: Drowning is different at the start
blocks.body: Give five initial rescue breaths for an unresponsive, non-normally-breathing drowning casualty, then continue CPR. A normal adult cardiac-arrest sequence does not begin with these five breaths.

lessons.title: Child & infant CPR
lessons.summary: Revise the differences in breaths, depth, technique and your training scope.

blocks.heading: First actions
blocks.body: Check responsiveness, call for help promptly, open the airway and check breathing for no more than ten seconds. Give five initial rescue breaths if the child or infant is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

blocks.heading: Technique
blocks.body: Compress the chest by at least one third of its depth: approximately 4 cm for an infant and 5 cm for a child. Aim for 100–120 compressions per minute and full recoil. Use the current two-thumb encircling technique for an infant; use one or two hands for a child as needed for effective depth.

blocks.heading: Choose the trained ratio
blocks.body: RCUK 2025 recommends 15:2 for rescuers specifically trained in paediatric basic life support; otherwise use 30:2. Do not choose a ratio solely by counting rescuers. Follow the sequence covered by your current qualification and the emergency call handler.

blocks.heading: AED for children
blocks.body: Use paediatric mode/pads when appropriate and available. Follow the device instructions; an AED can be used at any age. Pads must not touch each other. The front-and-back position may be needed for a small chest.

lessons.title: Using an AED safely
lessons.summary: Switch it on, attach pads and follow the prompts.

blocks.heading: Get it early
blocks.body: Send someone for the AED while care continues. Switch on the device and follow its spoken and visual instructions. Expose the chest and quickly dry the pad sites so pads adhere.

blocks.heading: Apply and analyse
blocks.body: Place the pads according to the diagrams on the pads/device. Where another rescuer is available, keep CPR going while pads are applied. Ensure nobody touches the casualty during analysis or shock delivery.

blocks.heading: Resume immediately
blocks.body: After a shock, or a no-shock instruction, restart CPR as directed. A no-shock message does not mean the person is well. Leave the AED attached and keep following its prompts.

blocks.heading: Poolside checks
blocks.body: Know the AED location, access arrangements, readiness indicator and how faults or expired pads are reported. Keep the recommended accessories nearby. Remove the casualty from the water before using an AED and follow local equipment training.

lessons.title: Unresponsive but breathing normally
lessons.summary: Keep the airway open and keep reassessing.

blocks.heading: When it applies
blocks.body: An unresponsive person needs urgent help. If they are breathing normally and do not need CPR, a side-lying recovery position can maintain the airway and allow fluid to drain. Continue to watch breathing and responsiveness.

blocks.heading: Trauma changes the decision
blocks.body: Do not automatically roll a person with suspected trauma into the recovery position. Current RCUK guidance advises avoiding this in trauma and prioritising airway opening while minimising spinal movement. If the airway cannot otherwise be maintained, use your trained assisted movement and emergency advice.

blocks.heading: Be ready to change
blocks.body: If breathing becomes absent or abnormal, place the casualty on their back and start CPR. Never leave them unattended or assume the recovery position removes the need for monitoring. Prevent heat loss and hand over to responders.

lessons.title: Choking: adults, children & infants
lessons.summary: Distinguish an effective cough from a severe airway obstruction.

blocks.heading: Effective cough
blocks.body: Ask if they are choking. If they can cough effectively, encourage coughing and observe closely. Do not hit their back while they are managing an effective cough, and do not give food or drink.

blocks.heading: Severe obstruction
blocks.body: If the cough is ineffective, give up to five back blows, checking after each. If unsuccessful, give up to five abdominal thrusts in adults and children, then alternate the two. Summon emergency help promptly if unresolved. For a visibly pregnant person, or when abdominal thrusts cannot be performed effectively, use the trained chest-thrust method.

blocks.heading: Infants
blocks.body: Never use abdominal thrusts on an infant. Use up to five back blows and then up to five chest thrusts using the current taught technique. Support the head and body throughout. Practise positioning on a manikin with your trainer.

blocks.heading: If they become unresponsive
blocks.body: Lower safely, ensure 999/112 has been called and begin age-appropriate resuscitation. Remove only an object you can clearly see and reach; never perform blind finger sweeps. Arrange medical assessment after abdominal thrusts or chest compressions.

lessons.title: Heart attack, stroke & fainting
lessons.summary: Recognise the pattern, call early and monitor for deterioration.

blocks.heading: Suspected heart attack
blocks.body: Chest pressure or tightness, pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, sweating, nausea and breathlessness can indicate a heart attack. Symptoms vary. Call 999/112, help the casualty rest comfortably, reassure them and monitor breathing. Assist with their prescribed medication within your training.

blocks.heading: FAST for stroke
blocks.body: Face: can they smile evenly? Arms: can they raise and hold both arms? Speech: is it slurred or unusual? Time: call 999/112 immediately if a stroke is suspected. Note when symptoms began or when they were last known well. Do not give food or drink if swallowing may be impaired.

blocks.heading: Fainting
blocks.body: Help a faint person lie down safely and monitor them. If appropriate and there is no injury or breathing difficulty, raise their legs. Do not assume every collapse is a simple faint: persistent unresponsiveness, abnormal breathing, chest pain or incomplete recovery needs urgent assessment.

lessons.title: Severe bleeding, internal bleeding & shock
lessons.summary: Control life-threatening bleeding and recognise failing circulation.

blocks.heading: Direct pressure first
blocks.body: Call 999/112 for serious bleeding. Use gloves and apply firm direct pressure with a dressing or clean material. If an object is embedded, do not pull it out; apply pressure around it and support it. Severe limb bleeding that remains uncontrolled may need a tourniquet or haemostatic dressing by a trained responder.

blocks.heading: Internal bleeding
blocks.body: A casualty can lose a dangerous amount of blood without an obvious wound. Suspect this after a significant impact or when there is worsening pallor, clamminess, weakness, confusion, swelling or collapse. Call urgently and monitor.

blocks.heading: Shock
blocks.body: Shock means inadequate circulation to vital organs. Treat the cause where possible, help the casualty lie down if appropriate, keep them warm and monitor breathing. Raise legs only if appropriate and injuries allow. Do not give food or drink; allow a comfortable supported position if breathing is difficult.

blocks.heading: Amputation
blocks.body: Control bleeding and call emergency services. Preserve the separated part in a clean wrapping inside a waterproof bag, cooled without direct ice contact or freezing, and send it with the casualty. Never delay treatment to search for it.

lessons.title: Cuts, grazes, bruises & nosebleeds
lessons.summary: Use clean treatment and recognise when an apparently small injury needs help.

blocks.heading: Cuts and grazes
blocks.body: Check for foreign material, irrigate with clean water, dry gently and cover with a suitable sterile dressing. Seek help for deep, contaminated or persistently bleeding wounds. Do not dig out embedded objects.

blocks.heading: Bruises and splinters
blocks.body: A wrapped cold pack can reduce discomfort and swelling; do not place ice directly on skin. A small visible superficial splinter may be removed with clean tweezers according to training. Seek help for deeply embedded material or signs of infection.

blocks.heading: Nosebleed
blocks.body: Sit the casualty forward and ask them to pinch the soft part of the nose continuously for 10–15 minutes, breathing through the mouth. Do not tilt the head back. Seek medical help for heavy or persistent bleeding, breathing difficulty or a significant injury.

lessons.title: Burns, scalds & electrical injury
lessons.summary: Stop exposure, cool a thermal burn and avoid adding further harm.

blocks.heading: Thermal burns
blocks.body: Cool the affected area under cool running water for 20 minutes. Remove nearby jewellery and loose clothing before swelling develops, but leave anything stuck to the burn. Keep the rest of the casualty warm.

blocks.heading: Cover and refer
blocks.body: After cooling, cover loosely with a non-adherent sterile dressing or cling film laid over the burn. Do not wrap tightly, burst blisters or apply creams, butter or ice. Obtain urgent help for large, deep, chemical or electrical burns, inhalation injury, critical areas or any serious concern.

blocks.heading: Electricity
blocks.body: Do not touch someone who may still be in contact with a live source. Arrange safe isolation and call for help. Once safe, assess responsiveness and breathing, provide CPR/AED if required and treat burns. Electrical injury can be serious despite a small visible wound.

blocks.heading: Severity matters
blocks.body: Size, depth, location, cause and the casualty’s age and condition all affect risk. Pain alone is not a reliable guide: a deep burn may damage nerves and be less painful.

lessons.title: Fractures, dislocations, sprains & strains
lessons.summary: Support the injury without forcing it back into place.

blocks.heading: Recognise injury
blocks.body: Pain, swelling, deformity, bruising, reduced movement or a wound over a bone can indicate a fracture. A dislocation changes the joint’s normal alignment. A sprain affects ligaments; a strain affects muscle or tendon.

blocks.heading: Support and seek help
blocks.body: Keep the casualty comfortable, support the injured part in the position found and avoid unnecessary movement. Use slings only as trained and check circulation beyond a bandage. Do not straighten a limb or try to relocate a joint.

blocks.heading: Soft-tissue care
blocks.body: Stop the activity, protect and support the injury and use a wrapped cold pack if appropriate. Refer when pain, swelling, deformity or loss of function suggests more than a minor injury. Cramp in the water can compromise swimming: assist the swimmer to safety before addressing the muscle.

lessons.title: Head, spinal & chest injuries
lessons.summary: Protect breathing and get urgent help for serious trauma.

blocks.heading: Head injury
blocks.body: Confusion, memory loss, vomiting, worsening headache, unequal pupils, seizure or reduced responsiveness after an impact are concerning. Stop activity and arrange medical assessment; call 999/112 for serious symptoms. Keep head, neck and body aligned as far as practical and monitor breathing.

blocks.heading: Chest injury
blocks.body: Painful or difficult breathing, an open chest wound or abnormal chest movement can be life-threatening. Call 999/112 and support the casualty in a comfortable position. Do not remove an embedded object.

blocks.heading: Open chest wounds
blocks.body: Current first-aid guidance advises leaving an open chest wound uncovered rather than sealing it with an improvised airtight dressing. Control local bleeding without obstructing airflow. Specialised vented dressings require suitable training.

blocks.heading: Airway over immobilisation
blocks.body: Minimise spinal movement, but never let a suspected spinal injury prevent an open airway or necessary resuscitation. Use the trained team approach and emergency call handler’s instructions.

lessons.title: Asthma & rapid breathing
lessons.summary: Support breathing and avoid assuming the cause is anxiety.

blocks.heading: Asthma
blocks.body: Wheeze, breathlessness, difficulty speaking and distress may indicate an asthma attack. Help the casualty sit comfortably and use their own reliever inhaler, with a spacer if available, according to their plan and your training.

blocks.heading: Escalate early
blocks.body: Call 999/112 for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, exhaustion, altered responsiveness, blue/grey colour, inability to speak normally or failure to improve. Continue monitoring and be ready to start CPR if they become unresponsive and breathing is abnormal.

blocks.heading: Hyperventilation
blocks.body: Rapid breathing, tingling and hand cramps can occur with anxiety, but may also accompany a serious illness. Reassure the casualty in a quiet setting and encourage slower, comfortable breathing. Do not use a paper bag. Seek urgent help when the cause is uncertain or symptoms are prolonged or severe.

lessons.title: Anaphylaxis & adrenaline auto-injectors
lessons.summary: Recognise a life-threatening allergic reaction and act immediately.

blocks.heading: Recognise the emergency
blocks.body: A rapid reaction after a trigger may cause swelling of the tongue or throat, noisy breathing, wheeze, faintness or collapse. Skin changes may occur, but do not wait for a rash before acting.

blocks.heading: Immediate actions
blocks.body: Call 999/112 and say “anaphylaxis”. Help the casualty use their prescribed adrenaline auto-injector promptly, or administer it within your training and authorisation. Follow the device’s printed instructions; different brands have different steps and hold times. Note the time.

blocks.heading: Position and repeat
blocks.body: Do not let the casualty stand or walk. Keep them lying down; if breathing is difficult they may sit with legs extended. If symptoms persist after five minutes, give a second dose if available, ideally in the opposite thigh. Continue monitoring and prepare for CPR.

blocks.heading: Handover
blocks.body: Tell responders the suspected trigger, timing of symptoms, changes in responsiveness and the number and times of injections. Give them the used devices safely. Emergency assessment is needed even if the person feels better.

lessons.title: Diabetic emergencies
lessons.summary: Low blood sugar can develop quickly, especially with exercise.

blocks.heading: Recognise low blood sugar
blocks.body: Shaking, sweating, hunger, confusion, dizziness and unusual behaviour can progress to reduced responsiveness. Ask about diabetes and relevant medication when the person can respond.

blocks.heading: If awake and swallowing safely
blocks.body: Help them take a fast-acting source of sugar, such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink, according to their care plan and training. A diet drink does not provide the required sugar. Reassess; call emergency services if they worsen or do not improve.

blocks.heading: If unresponsive
blocks.body: Call 999/112, assess breathing and provide appropriate emergency care. Never put food, drink or glucose gel into an unresponsive person’s mouth. Do not administer insulin as a first-aid treatment.

blocks.heading: High blood sugar
blocks.body: Excessive thirst, frequent urination, drowsiness and sometimes fruity-smelling breath may develop more gradually. Serious illness or altered responsiveness needs urgent help. Do not try to diagnose the blood-sugar level from appearance alone.

lessons.title: Seizures in water & on land
lessons.summary: Prevent injury, protect the airway and time the seizure.

blocks.heading: On land
blocks.body: Clear nearby hazards, cushion the head and note the start and finish time. Do not restrain the person, put anything in their mouth or give food or drink during the seizure. Stay with them.

blocks.heading: In water
blocks.body: Summon help and use your trained rescue method to keep the face clear of water. Protect the head from striking the side. Arrange safe removal and urgent assessment, especially after possible water inhalation.

blocks.heading: After movements stop
blocks.body: Check breathing. If absent or abnormal, begin CPR. If breathing normally, protect the airway and monitor closely, taking any trauma into account. Reassure them as awareness returns.

blocks.heading: When to call
blocks.body: Call 999/112 for a first seizure, one lasting longer than usual or more than five minutes when the usual duration is unknown, repeated seizures without recovery, serious injury, breathing difficulty or uncertainty. In a pool incident, follow the EAP and consider drowning risk.

lessons.title: Heat exhaustion, heatstroke & hypothermia
lessons.summary: Move away from the cause and watch for altered responsiveness.

blocks.heading: Heat illness
blocks.body: Move a person with heat exhaustion into a cool place, remove excess clothing and cool them. If fully alert and able to swallow, offer cool fluids. Confusion, collapse or severe deterioration in hot conditions may be heatstroke: call 999/112 and begin active cooling promptly.

blocks.heading: Hypothermia
blocks.body: A cold casualty may shiver, become slow, confused or drowsy. Move to shelter, gently remove wet clothing when practical and insulate with dry layers, including from the ground. Handle carefully and seek urgent help for significant symptoms.

blocks.heading: Avoid harmful shortcuts
blocks.body: Do not rub cold limbs or apply intense direct heat. Give a warm drink only when fully alert and able to swallow safely. Continue to assess breathing and responsiveness; begin CPR if indicated.

lessons.title: Eyes, teeth, poisoning & stings
lessons.summary: Remove the source safely and get the right help.

blocks.heading: Eye injuries
blocks.body: Do not let the casualty rub the eye. Irrigate loose contamination with clean water. For a chemical splash, begin continuous irrigation immediately, keeping contaminated water away from the other eye, and obtain urgent medical help. Do not remove a penetrating object.

blocks.heading: Dental injuries
blocks.body: Handle a knocked-out permanent tooth by its crown, not its root, and obtain urgent dental care. Keep it moist, commonly in milk if it cannot safely be replaced by a suitably informed person. Do not reinsert a baby tooth. Preserve broken fragments for the dentist.

blocks.heading: Poisoning
blocks.body: Poisons can be swallowed, inhaled, injected or absorbed. Avoid exposure yourself, call for urgent help and provide the product details where safe. Do not induce vomiting or give an improvised neutralising substance. Follow the call handler and the site’s chemical procedure.

blocks.heading: Stings
blocks.body: Remove a visible sting promptly using your trained method and cool the area with a wrapped cold pack. Watch for anaphylaxis, particularly with airway swelling, breathing problems or faintness. A sting in the mouth or throat needs urgent attention.

lessons.title: Secondary survey, handover & incident records
lessons.summary: Gather useful information without delaying urgent care.

blocks.heading: History, symptoms and signs
blocks.body: History is what happened and relevant medical background. Symptoms are what the casualty tells you they feel. Signs are what you observe. Ask about allergies, medication and previous conditions when appropriate.

blocks.heading: Head-to-toe examination
blocks.body: Once immediate threats are managed, check for other injuries with consent and dignity. Look for bleeding, deformity, swelling and tenderness. Revisit the primary survey whenever the condition changes; finding a minor injury must not distract from worsening breathing.

blocks.heading: Movement
blocks.body: Move an injured person only when necessary for safety or treatment. Consider injuries, their ability to help, the route, equipment and staff available. Use trained handling methods and clear coordination.

blocks.heading: Handover and records
blocks.body: Provide facts: what happened, timing, findings, changes, treatment and response. Record promptly and confidentially, including witnesses where appropriate. Report through the operator’s procedure; the responsible person determines any external reporting duties. Replenish equipment and take part in a constructive debrief.
